notes: Wikidata P569 confirmed: +1926-04-29T00:00:00Z. Born in Grodno, then Second Polish Republic (now Belarus).
Wikidata P570 confirmed. Died in Palo Alto, California, from complications of lung cancer.

Joined RAND 1959; Wikipedia states 'essentially all the work was defined by 1961, and fleshed out and put into formal written form in 1962'. First published RAND report 1960. Conceived = year he began the survivable-network work.
'On Distributed Communications' 11-volume RAND report series (RM-3420) published 1964 — the formulated/completed work. Core concept written 1962 (RAND P-2626).
Born 7 June 1924 in Treorchy, Rhondda Valley, Wales. Wikipedia infobox; no Wikidata ID confirmed in this harvest.
Died 28 May 2000 in Esher, Surrey, England.
Davies 'became interested in data communications after attending the IFIP Congress in New York in 1965' — inception of his packet-switching concept. Independent of Baran's earlier work.

Davies coined the term 'packet switching' in 1965-1966. Wikipedia: 'He coined the term packet switching, and proposed building a commercial nationwide data network in the UK.' Consulted a linguist for a term translatable across languages.
Joined NPL in 1947 per Wikipedia. Inhabited act-npl from this date.
Formally retired from NPL in 1984. 'Relinquished management responsibilities in 1979' to focus on research, then retired 1984.
Born June 13, 1934, New York City. Wikipedia infobox.

Thesis proposal 'Information Flow in Large Communication Nets' (1961) initiated doctoral research applying queueing theory to network delays. His 1964 book 'Communication Nets' published. Note: this is the queueing-theory work, NOT packet-switching conception (which is disputed per specimen discrepancies[1]).
Wikidata P569: +1943-06-23T00:00:00Z, precision day. Born in New Haven, Connecticut (per Wikipedia).
PhD from UCLA 1972; assistant professor at Stanford 1972-1976. Active in internetworking from 1972 onwards.

Cerf and Kahn published 'A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication' (IEEE Trans. Comms, May 1974). RFC 675 published December 1974 — first use of term 'internet'. This is the formulation date of TCP/IP internetworking.
Born December 23, 1938, New York City. Wikipedia infobox.
Kahn 'worked with Vint Cerf beginning spring 1973 to develop TCP/IP protocols'. Kahn's open-architecture problem articulated 1973 when he needed to connect ARPANET + SATNET + ALOHANET.
Founded CNRI (Corporation for National Research Initiatives) in 1986 after leaving DARPA. Remains chairman, CEO, and president as of 2022.
Born 20 April 1931 in Chantenay-Saint-Imbert, Nièvre, France. Wikipedia infobox. Categorized 'Living people' as of Jan 2026 update.

CYCLADES project planning began 1971 at IRIA (French national computer science institute). Pouzin directed the project. The datagram concept (term coined by Halvor Bothner-By but architecture by Pouzin) emerged from this work in early 1970s.
CYCLADES project planning began 1971. Design and staffing began 1972. First demonstration November 1973 (three hosts and one packet switch). Full deployment with 20 nodes 1976.

'By 1981, Cyclades was forced to shut down.' France's PTT (DGT) refused to fund a competitor to Transpac/Minitel and 'insisted that the permission and funding be rescinded.' The network went offline 1981.
Born March 11, 1915, St. Louis, Missouri. Wikipedia infobox.
Died June 26, 1990, Arlington, Massachusetts.

'Intergalactic Computer Network' memos: formulated at BBN in August 1962; memorandum distributed April 23, 1963. First IPTO director October 1962 - July 1964. The internetworking vision (conjecture-in-a-parent) dates to this memo.
First IPTO director from October 1962.
Left IPTO July 1964 (first term). Had a second IPTO term 1974-1975. Retired as professor emeritus 1985.
Bob Taylor born February 10, 1932, Dallas, Texas. (The specimen node act-roberts-taylor covers both Taylor and Roberts; this fact is for Taylor.)
Bob Taylor died April 13, 2017, Woodside, California.
Larry Roberts (separate from Taylor in act-roberts-taylor node). Born December 21, 1937, Westport, Connecticut. Proposed node as the specimen merges Taylor+Roberts into one actor.
Larry Roberts died December 26, 2018, Redwood City, California.
Taylor named IPTO director by June 1966; Roberts joined ARPA in late 1966. The node's ARPANET-launch period begins 1966.
Born October 15, 1944. Wikipedia infobox; birthplace not specified in article.
RFC 1 ('Host Software') published April 7, 1969 by Steve Crocker of UCLA. This is the founding date of the RFC process (sw-rfc-method). The date is well-attested in the literature.
Born April 7, 1944. Wikipedia infobox; birthplace not specified.

IAB chief protocol architect 1981-1989. End-to-end principle paper presented April 8-10, 1981 at Second International Conference on Distributed Computing Systems, Paris (co-authored with Saltzer and Reed).
'We reject kings, presidents and voting; we believe in rough consensus and running code' — Clark's famous dictum, 1992. This is the naming/articulation date of the IETF process ethos (sw-rfc-method).
Born 8 June 1955, London, England. Wikipedia infobox.
World Wide Web proposal submitted to CERN management: 12 March 1989. First website published 20 December 1990. W3C founded 1994 at MIT.
Returned to CERN as fellow in 1984 (had a first stint June-December 1980 as independent contractor). Active at CERN 1984-1994.
ARPA established February 7, 1958 by President Eisenhower in response to Sputnik (October 4, 1957). Renamed DARPA in March 1972, back to ARPA February 1993, back to DARPA March 1996.
Leo Beranek and Richard Bolt established their partnership at MIT on October 15, 1948. ARPANET IMP contract awarded August 1968; first IMP shipped to UCLA September 1969.

Raytheon completed acquisition of BBN on October 29, 2009 (~$350M). BBN became RTX BBN Technologies, a subsidiary of RTX Corporation (formerly Raytheon). Effective dissolution of the independent company.
NPL established 1900 at Bushy House, Teddington, for standardizing instruments and determining physical constants. First packet-switched network implemented there early 1969, operational 1970.
NSF established May 10, 1950 when President Truman signed Public Law 507 (the National Science Foundation Act of 1950).
NSFNET 'initiated operations in 1986' with 56 kbit/s backbone connecting six supercomputing center sites, using TCP/IP. Program authorized 1985, operational 1986.

NSFNET Backbone Service decommissioned April 30, 1995, 'successfully transitioned to a new architecture' of commercial ISPs and Network Access Points (NAPs). This is also the consolidation/hardening date for child-internet.

IETF first meeting January 16, 1986, attended by 21 US federal government-funded researchers. Emerged from the Gateway Algorithms and Data Structures (GADS) Task Force, divided by the Internet Activities Board (IAB) that month. Transitioned to Internet Society sponsorship in 1993.
INWG established June 1972 in Paris by Steve Crocker, Louis Pouzin, Donald Davies, and Peter Kirstein. Vint Cerf became chair in October 1972.

INWG 'continued to work on protocol design and formal specification until the 1990s when it disbanded as the Internet grew rapidly.' Exact dissolution date not specified; approximate decade given. Certainty low for specific date.
CERN established 29 September 1954 by twelve Western European countries. The acronym originally stood for 'Conseil Européen pour la Recherche Nucléaire'.
Cisco founded December 10, 1984 by Leonard Bosack and Sandy Lerner, both Stanford University computer scientists. Commercialized the multi-protocol router they had developed at Stanford.
Internet Society (ISOC) founded December 11, 1992 by Vint Cerf, Bob Kahn, and Lyman Chapin. Vint Cerf served as first president. IETF moved under ISOC sponsorship in 1993.

ICANN incorporated September 30, 1998 as a California nonprofit corporation. Esther Dyson served as founding chairwoman. Emerged from US DoC Green Paper (February 20, 1998) proposing privatization of Internet name/address management. Transitioned to global multistakeholder control October 1, 2016.
X.25 standard finalized in 'The Orange Book' 1976 by CCITT; unanimous approval at the CCITT plenary September 1976. The primary rival virtual-circuit packet standard.

Beginning early 1990s, X.25 networks in North America started being replaced by Frame Relay, then IP. Minitel (X.25-based) shut down June 30, 2012. X.25 persists in niche use (aviation, amateur radio); BT still offered it commercially as of 2019. Status: 'niche' — not fully faded but displaced as mainstream.

ISO initiated OSI program in 1977. Hubert Zimmermann first defined the OSI model 'in raw form' in Washington, D.C., February 1978. Draft standard published by ISO 1980. Formalized/published as ISO 7498 in 1984.
OSI model officially published 1984 by both ISO (as ISO 7498) and CCITT. CCITT and ISO documents merged to form the formal standard in May 1983.

OSI protocols never gained significant adoption; 'still used as a reference for teaching and documentation' only. TCP/IP won the protocol wars ~1990-1995. GOSIP mandate dropped 1994-95. OSI stack faded; the model persists as pedagogical reference only. Status: 'faded'.

PTT initiated design of the Minitel network in 1978. Experimental launch July 15, 1980 in Saint-Malo with 55 customers. Commercial service launched nationwide 1982. By 1984 free terminals distributed to French households.

Minitel service 'was discontinued by France Télécom on 30 June 2012.' 800,000 terminals still in operation at shutdown. Operated over the Transpac X.25 network. The rival-lifecycle-coupling irony: the datagram CYCLADES pioneered defeated Minitel globally.
Minitel definitively shut down June 30, 2012, displaced by the Internet. Status: 'faded' (completely discontinued, not niche).

ARPANET became operational 1969; first four-node configuration established by December 5, 1969 (UCLA, Stanford Research Institute, UC Santa Barbara, University of Utah). First IMP installed at UCLA. Declared operational 1971.

'The ARPANET project was formally decommissioned in 1990.' Wikipedia: 'In the wake of the decommissioning of the ARPANET on 28 February 1990' Vint Cerf wrote his farewell poem. Some equipment remained until July 1990.

Donald Davies at NPL coined the term 'packet switching' in 1965-1966. Paul Baran's earlier work (1959-1964) used 'distributed adaptive message block switching'. The term 'packet' chosen after consulting a linguist to ensure translatability.

The Wikipedia article on Louis Pouzin states the term 'datagram' was 'named by Halvor Bothner-By', not Pouzin himself. Pouzin viewed the architecture as his invention. Approximate date 1973 based on CYCLADES operational timeline. Certainty reduced due to attribution uncertainty around exact coining.

Cerf and Kahn published 'A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication' May 1974. RFC 675 ('Specification of Internet Transmission Control Program', written by Cerf, Yogen Dalal, Carl Sunshine) published December 1974 — contains first attested use of the term 'internet'.
In TCP/IP version 4 (1978), the monolithic Transmission Control Program was divided into TCP and IP — the split that created the narrow waist / IP-as-universal-datagram-layer.

'End-to-End Arguments in System Design' presented at Second International Conference on Distributed Computing Systems, Paris, April 8-10, 1981. Authors: J.H. Saltzer, D.P. Reed, D.D. Clark. Updated/published in ACM Transactions on Computer Systems 1984. CYCLADES had practiced the principle earlier (1970s).

RFC 1 'Host Software' published April 7, 1969 by Steve Crocker (UCLA). Founded the RFC process / open standardization method. Today official publication channel for IETF, IAB, and the global networking research community.
World Wide Web proposal submitted to CERN March 12, 1989. First website published December 20, 1990 (info.cern.ch). CERN made the Web royalty-free / public domain April 30, 1993. W3C founded 1994.
Flag day: January 1, 1983 — NCP to TCP/IP cutover on the ARPANET. 'TCP/IP protocols became the standard for the ARPANET' on this date. Operationally complete by June 1983.
NSFNET initiated operations 1986 with 56 kbit/s backbone; scaled the internetwork beyond defense to research/education. Commercial traffic allowed from 1991. Backbone retired April 30, 1995.

notes: IPTO (Information Processing Techniques Office) established within ARPA in 1962; Licklider was its first director, October 1962. The office that ran the networking program through the cascade. Dissolved or merged ~1986 when DARPA reorganized.

ESTIMATE: Specimen states IPTO 'when: 1962-1986'. Wikipedia page for IPTO not directly fetched in this harvest; date taken from specimen text. Certainty reduced. Prefix ESTIMATE: the 1986 dissolution date is from the specimen itself, not from a separately fetched source.

ISO (founded 1947) and CCITT (founded 1956) are long-standing bodies. Their NETWORKED-STANDARDS role (OSI+X.25) began with the X.25 standard 1976 (CCITT) and the OSI program 1977 (ISO). This fact records the inception of their role in the Internet specimen's rival-standard lineage.
Baran joined RAND 1959; work on survivable/distributed networks began then. First RAND report published 1960; core work 'essentially all defined by 1961'.
Davies independently conceived packet switching in 1965 after attending IFIP Congress in New York. Term 'packet' coined 1965-1966.

'End-to-End Arguments in System Design' by Saltzer, Reed, Clark formally presented April 1981 and published in ACM Trans. Computer Systems 1984. The principle was practiced in CYCLADES from early 1970s, formally articulated 1981.

Kahn articulated the open-architecture problem in 1973 when he needed to connect ARPANET + SATNET + ALOHANET. The four ground rules (each network stands on its own; no internal change required; best-effort with end-host recovery; no global control) were formulated at this point.

CYCLADES project began 1971-1972; Pouzin developed the datagram/connectionless model during this period. Pouzin coined 'catenet' in 1973. Note: Wikipedia says 'datagram' term was named by Halvor Bothner-By, not Pouzin; the architecture/approach was Pouzin's.

First IMP (Interface Message Processor) delivered to UCLA in September 1969. First ARPANET message sent October 29, 1969 (UCLA to SRI). Four-node configuration by December 5, 1969. BBN IMP contract awarded August 1968.

NSFNET Backbone Service retired April 30, 1995 — the commercialization date that hardened the Internet into a global utility. Commercial ISPs assumed backbone function via Network Access Points (NAPs).

RFC 675 (December 1974) contains 'the first attested use of the term internet, as a shorthand for internetwork'. Authors: Vint Cerf, Yogen Dalal, Carl Sunshine. The term 'Internet' (capitalized) became standard usage later.
Stanford's role in TCP/IP development begins with Cerf's assistant professorship 1972-1976. UCLA was ARPANET node 1 (1969). UCL (UK) was first international ARPANET node.
NSFNET program authorized in 1985; operations initiated 1986. Distinct from the NSF agency (act-nsf, founded 1950); this is the NSFNET infrastructure program that scaled the Internet 1986-1995.

Kleinrock published 'Communication Nets: Stochastic Message Flow and Delay' 1964, the book form of his queueing-theory work. PhD dissertation 1963 at MIT. Note: this is queueing theory for message networks — the contested packet-switching claim is recorded separately at 0.5 confidence per specimen discrepancies[1].
Cerf and Kahn co-founded the Internet Society (ISOC) in 1992; Cerf served as first president. This is a key institutionalization date for act-cerf's governance role.

In 1993 IETF 'changed from an activity supported by the US federal government to an independent, international activity associated with the Internet Society.' The transition from government-funded to ISOC-sponsored is the key maturation event. IETF continues operating, so this is active_to for the US-government-funded phase.
